Replace your plan and cases?
Uploading a cases file replaces the plan on screen and all your saved cases with the ones in the file. What you have now can’t be brought back, so use Download cases first if you want to keep it. If the file is damaged, doesn’t follow the cases file template (a field missing, added or of the wrong kind), or can’t be loaded, nothing changes.
Simulating 5,000 markets…

Predicted growth

Plan: your household’s withdrawals

Plan sets the household’s withdrawals from every account, and when CPP and OAS start, so each retired year’s cash flow is as steady as it can be. Nothing changes until you click Apply plan.

  • The steady level comes from your own settings (spending, income, accounts, your points and contributions): what must come out anyway is spread evenly, and the rest stays invested. When your savings can’t keep up, the plan is a steady shortfall every year instead of running out at the end.
  • How it chooses: the steadiest plan first (the household, then each of you), then the one with the fewest jumps (in retirement, a year or three well off the years around it; while you work, any change, such as CPP or OAS paid before work stops), then the least spending left unpaid, then the most for you and your estate: your surplus plus the estate after tax. A plan is offered only if it beats your plan now; if none does, the card says so and your plan stays.
  • What it tries: every start age, a year at a time, and ways of drawing: how much RRSP and RRIF income each of you takes before the other accounts (seven ceilings, one before and one after your CPP and OAS are both paid), the RRIF or Non-registered first or half each, and before 65 sharing it so your incomes come out about the same. Hundreds of plans run on a quick model; the best are then checked in the 5,000 markets.
  • A later start pays more for life but nothing until then, so it’s worth it only with a long life: the plan assumes you live to its end. To keep your own ages, untick Plan chooses CPP and OAS start ages.
  • Your points stay as they are. Plan adds points of its own (hollow circles) to the account lines only, never to income, spending or contributions; planning again replaces only Plan’s.
  • Dollars: the steady level is in today’s dollars, so in each year’s dollars it rises with the inflation you set, keeping what it buys the same. The tiles are in today’s dollars; Show amounts in draws the charts in today’s dollars or each year’s.
  • The charts show Plan solid and your plan now dashed: Cash flow (the household’s surplus, or each person’s net income, with a pension income split counted with the one who reports it), Account balances at each year end (how often an account runs short in the 5,000 markets; 5,000 markets draws them), CPP and OAS each year, and the Estate after tax if both of you, or each of you, died that year.
  • Why some years stand out: under the Cash flow chart, the card explains up to four years that jump well above or below the years around them, or sit well off the steady level (numbered on the chart). For each: what changes that year, why Plan can’t even it out, and one or two things you could try. Plan can’t change a working year, money that must come out (a RRIF minimum, or one of your points), or accounts that are empty or held by contributions or your points. An account still getting contributions isn’t drawn while it does, so ending them sooner lets Plan even out more. A red note names a point of yours Plan couldn’t keep within reach.

      Ask an AI assistant for your portfolio’s metrics

      “I hold a portfolio of [Percentage]% [Ticker/Company], [Percentage]% [Ticker/Company], and [Percentage]% [Ticker/Company]. Based on [Number] years of historical data, what are my portfolio’s average annual capital gain, standard deviation, and distribution yield?”

      Note: You can include as many holdings as you like—just ensure the weights sum to 100% and the tickers or company names are valid.

      Examples:

      Single holding:

      “I have a portfolio of 100% VFV.TO. Using 8 years of history, what are my portfolio’s average annual capital gain, standard deviation, and distribution yield?”

      Multi-asset allocation:

      “I have a portfolio of 40% Royal Bank, 35% Enbridge, and 25% Telus. Using 10 years of history, what are my portfolio’s average annual capital gain, standard deviation, and distribution yield?”

      Retirement Financial Planner

      Text size

      What is this app?

      • A Canadian retirement planner: your income, tax, savings and estate, year by year.
      • Covers CPP, QPP, OAS, GIS, RRSPs, RRIFs, TFSAs and tax in every province and territory.
      • Runs in your browser; your numbers never leave your computer.

      Why you need it

      • Planning for an uncertain future is hard and stressful. Whether you’re planning your own retirement or helping clients with theirs, the app lays out the whole picture year by year, so you can test each idea before any real money moves.
      • Makes complex decisions easier by letting you compare financial scenarios built on numbers, not on guesses and feelings.
      • Helps you explore, with confidence, ways to reduce costs, increase income, smooth cash flow and manage risk and uncertainty.

      How to make the most of it

      • Start with one of the four demo cases, try some changes and compare the plans side by side.
      • Let Plan withdrawals find your steadiest cash flow.
      • Review your plan from time to time.

      Questions and answers

      Will my money last?
      Do I have enough to retire? How much can I spend each year?
      1. Check your costs in Spending. They start at Statistics Canada averages for senior households like yours.
      2. Enter all your income and accounts.
      3. In Investment balances, drag each account’s end point down to $0, or to what you want to keep.
      4. In Cash flow and tax, on Combined (or You if you’re single), compare the Net income bar (what you can spend) with the orange spending bar. The third bar is your surplus, or a red shortfall.
      5. If it falls short, try working longer, starting CPP or OAS later, keeping less at the end or spending less. Save each try as a case.
      6. Or click Plan withdrawals: it finds the steadiest yearly surplus your savings can keep up.
      How long will my savings last?
      1. Set Years to plan (in You and your household) to reach the age you expect to live to, up to 30 years.
      2. In Investment balances, add a $0 point to an account in the year it should last until.
      3. Point at its line to see each year’s withdrawal (or click a year in Cash flow and tax with Show income by source ticked).
      4. Move the $0 point left or right until the withdrawal is what you need. That year is when the money runs out.
      Will my money last if markets do badly?
      1. In Investment accounts (panel 5 on the Today’s Finances tab), set each account’s Market outcome to Worst: only 1 market in 20 does worse.
      2. The app works out the smaller withdrawals that still reach your points in that market.
      3. In Cash flow and tax, check that the Net income bar still covers the orange spending bar. If it does, your plan holds up.
      4. To see all 5,000 markets for an account, click Predict above its chart in Investment balances.
      What if I retire early, or work part-time first?
      1. In Income, pick Employment income (1).
      2. Shape its line with points. For $90,000 now, $40,000 part-time from 62 and nothing from 65: add points at 61 ($90,000), 62 ($40,000), 64 ($40,000) and 65 ($0).
      3. Points a year apart make sudden changes; delete the in-between points for a gradual slope.
      4. Set Plan to retire at (in You and your household) to mark the year on the charts.
      5. Save a case for each plan and compare them in Planned Cases.
      How does inflation affect my plan?
      1. Your inflation setting raises CPP, OAS, withdrawals between your points, tax brackets and credits, and household costs every year.
      2. Employment, pension and other income stay as you enter them. If your pension is indexed, add points with rising amounts.
      3. Amounts are in each year’s dollars. To take inflation out, choose Today’s dollars under Show amounts in (Cash flow and tax, Account balances and estate).
      4. On an account’s Predict card, the Inflation line shows your balance now raised by inflation.

      Taking money out of your accounts
      How do I take money out of an account?
      1. You set balances, not withdrawals. In Investment balances, pick the account, then click its line in a later year to add a point, or drag a point down.
      2. The app compares your point with what the balance would grow to by then: growth from the account’s product and Market outcome, plus any contributions. If your point is lower, the app works out the yearly withdrawal that gets there, rising each year with inflation.
      3. A point can’t be higher than the balance could grow to.
      4. To see each year’s withdrawal, point at the line or click a point. It’s also in Cash flow and tax, with Show income by source ticked.
      5. It doesn’t work in years you still contribute to that account (the dotted part of the line). End the contributions first, in Investment contributions.
      6. Or click Plan withdrawals: it sets the points for you.
      Which account should I draw from first?
      1. Set the order with each account’s points in Investment balances. For example, to spend the RRIF first and keep the TFSA, drag the RRIF down to $0 early and leave the TFSA’s end point alone.
      2. Save a case, then try the opposite order and save again.
      3. Compare lifetime net income, tax and the final estate in Planned Cases.
      4. Keep in mind: RRSP and RRIF withdrawals are fully taxed and count for the clawback and GIS; TFSA withdrawals don’t; Non-registered withdrawals are taxed only on their dividends and gains.
      Should I draw down my RRSP before 71?
      1. In Investment balances, pick RRSP (8) and add a lower point earlier, for example $0 at 65.
      2. In that point’s card, set To RRIF (%): 100% moves the money to the RRIF tax-free; less turns that share into taxable spending now, when your income may be low.
      3. The card’s last section shows the added tax and clawback.
      4. Compare the Tax bars and the estate across cases.
      5. Or click Plan withdrawals: it draws the RRSP first, through the RRIF, moving only what it draws each year, so the rest stays invested until 71.
      I’m still saving. When can I start withdrawals?
      1. In Investment contributions, set each account’s yearly contribution, and end it with a $0 point in the first year you stop.
      2. In Investment balances, the account’s line is dotted in the years you contribute. Withdrawals can start the year after the last one.
      3. Add a lower point after those years to plan them, for example $0 at 90.
      4. Contributions count as spending in Cash flow and tax, so the surplus shows what’s left after saving.

      Government rules and benefits
      When should I start CPP (or QPP)?
      1. In Income, pick CPP (11) (QPP in Quebec).
      2. Drag the middle point to start at 65, and the last point to the yearly amount on your My Service Canada Account statement.
      3. The chart shows each year’s dollars, so it reads higher: $12,000 today is about $15,700 in 2036 at 2.75% inflation.
      4. Drag the start to 60 or 70. The app applies the official changes: 0.6% less for each month before 65 (−36% at 60), 0.7% more for each month after (+42% at 70).
      5. Save a case for each start age and compare lifetime net income in Planned Cases. A later start pays off only if you live long enough.
      6. Or click Plan withdrawals: it tries the start ages and picks the one with the steadiest cash flow.
      Should I delay OAS to 70?
      1. In Income, pick OAS (12).
      2. Drag the middle point to start OAS at any age from 65 to 70. Each month of delay adds 0.6%, up to 36% at 70.
      3. Save a case for each start age and compare them in Planned Cases.
      4. Delaying can help if your income in your late 60s is high enough for a clawback, but not if you’d get GIS, which starts only with OAS.
      5. Or let Plan withdrawals try the OAS and CPP start ages for the steadiest cash flow.
      Will I lose some of my OAS to the clawback?
      1. Know the rule: the clawback (the OAS recovery tax) takes 15% of your net income above about $95,300 (2026, rising with inflation).
      2. See it on the OAS chart (12): the dashed “After clawback” line is what’s left, and each year’s card shows the clawback.
      3. It’s also in the Tax bar in Cash flow and tax, and on its own in Data download.
      4. To lower it, draw down your RRSP or RRIF in lower-income years before OAS starts, take more from your TFSA (it isn’t income), or delay OAS.
      5. RRSP contributions, up to the year you turn 71, lower your income too.
      6. On the RRSP and RRIF charts, in Investment balances, a point’s card shows the “Added recovery tax (clawback)” its withdrawal causes.
      Can I get GIS or other benefits?
      1. You don’t enter them: the app works out GIS (13), the Allowance for a spouse aged 60 to 64 (14) and provincial top-ups (15) from your income each year.
      2. To see them, tick Show income by source in Cash flow and tax. They appear when your income is low enough.
      3. Pension, CPP, interest, dividends, RRSP and RRIF income reduce them; TFSA withdrawals don’t, so a TFSA can help you keep GIS. RRSP contributions lower that income.
      How does my RRSP become a RRIF?
      1. The rule: an RRSP must end by December 31 of the year you turn 71. On the RRSP chart (8), in Investment balances, it reaches $0 that year (the amber line), and what’s left moves to the RRIF.
      2. To move it sooner, add a lower RRSP point earlier, for example $0 at 65. The app takes it out gradually up to that point.
      3. Click an RRSP point to set its To RRIF (%), which applies from its year until the next RRSP point: 100% moves what leaves the RRSP to the RRIF tax-free; less makes that share taxable income now.
      4. Nothing leaves the RRSP while you still contribute to it. After your last contribution, what leaves moves 100% to the RRIF until your next RRSP point.
      5. The money arriving shows on the RRIF chart (9). The RRIF pays its minimum from the next year on (see the next question).
      6. Or click Plan withdrawals: it moves only what it draws each year, so the rest stays in the RRSP until 71.
      How do I manage my RRIF withdrawals?
      1. Each year, from the year after money arrives, the RRIF pays at least its minimum: a share of its January 1 balance that rises with age, for example 5.28% at 71 and 20% from 95.
      2. With no points of your own, the RRIF pays just the minimum. Its chart is RRIF (9), in Investment balances.
      3. To take more, add a lower point in a later year, or drag one down. If it’s lower than the balance after growth and the minimums, the app adds the extra withdrawal needed, rising each year with inflation. It never takes less than the minimum.
      4. Click a point, or point at the line, to see that year’s minimum, the withdrawal, and the tax and clawback it adds.
      5. If your spouse is younger, tick RRIF minimum by younger spouse’s age in You and your household for a smaller minimum.
      6. From 65, RRIF withdrawals get the pension income credit, and a couple can split them on their tax returns.

      Tax and your estate
      How much tax will I pay in retirement?
      1. In Cash flow and tax, the amber Tax bar below $0 is each year’s federal and provincial tax plus any OAS clawback, after the age, pension and dividend credits.
      2. Point at a year to see it in the list, or click it for its card. Choose Combined for the household.
      3. Compare lifetime tax, in today’s dollars, across plans in Planned Cases.
      4. For the full breakdown, use Data download.
      How much tax does an RRSP contribution save?
      1. Save a case first, so you can compare.
      2. Set the RRSP contribution in Investment contributions. It’s deducted from that year’s income, so it lowers your tax at your top rate and any OAS clawback, and can raise GIS.
      3. Compare the Tax in Cash flow and tax: point at the year, or click it.
      4. The money is taxed later, when it leaves the RRSP or RRIF as spending; a transfer to the RRIF isn’t taxed.
      5. The app doesn’t check your contribution room: see your Notice of Assessment or CRA My Account.
      Should I sell my Non-registered gains every year, or hold?
      1. In Investment accounts (panel 5 on the Today’s Finances tab), choose the Non-registered account’s Portfolio strategy. A new plan starts with Hold all time.
      2. Hold all time taxes gains only on what you sell, and the rest at death. Realize gains every year taxes each year’s growth that year, so no tax bill builds up.
      3. Either way, the tax is paid from your cash, as in real life, and shows in the Tax bar.
      4. Save a case for each and compare: the withdrawals if you set an end balance, or the final balance and estate if not.
      How much will I leave to my heirs, after tax?
      1. In Account balances and estate, tick Estate for heirs. The amber bar is what heirs would get after tax if you (You), your spouse (Spouse) or both of you (Combined) died that year.
      2. RRSP and RRIF balances are taxed in full, unsold Non-registered gains as if sold, and a TFSA passes tax-free. Probate fees come off the Non-registered balance.
      3. Compare the final estate, in today’s dollars, in Planned Cases.
      4. To leave more, try plans that spend the RRSP and RRIF first and keep the TFSA.

      Using the app
      I’m already retired. How do I enter my CPP, OAS and pension?
      1. CPP and OAS: if you already receive them, all three points sit at the start of the chart. Drag the last point to the yearly amount you get now.
      2. Workplace pension: drag the first point of Pension and annuity (2) to its yearly amount, and add points if it will rise.
      3. Accounts: in Investment balances, drag each account’s first point to your balance now.
      4. Or type this year’s amounts in the Today’s Finances form; the charts follow.
      Where do I enter interest and dividends from savings outside my accounts?
      1. Interest from GICs, bonds or savings held outside the accounts you enter here: type the yearly amount before tax in Taxable interest (3). It’s on your T5 slip, box 13. It’s taxed in full.
      2. Dividends from Canadian companies: type the actual amount you received in Canadian dividends (4), from T5 box 24, not the taxable amount in box 25. The app grosses it up by 38% and gives you the dividend tax credits, as your tax return does.
      3. Dividends from small private companies (other than eligible, T5 box 10) and foreign dividends: enter them in Other taxable income (5).
      4. Money in an account you entered here, such as the Non-registered account, earns its own yield: don’t enter that income again.
      5. Type this year’s amounts in Income on Today’s Finances, or shape them over the years on their charts in Income (Retirement Planner).
      How do I set up an investment product and use it for my accounts?
      1. On the Investment Products tab, click Add product.
      2. Enter its name, average annual capital gain, standard deviation and distribution yield (after fees), and a note if you like. Then click Save.
      3. Not sure of the numbers? Click How to find a product’s numbers on the same tab.
      4. In Investment accounts (panel 5 on the Today’s Finances tab), pick the product in an account’s Product list. Its numbers are copied into that account.
      5. To start new plans with it, choose it under Default product for each account.
      6. Your list stays in this browser: Download products saves a copy, and Upload products brings it back.
      How can I see how my investments might perform?
      1. On the Retirement Planner tab, in Investment balances, pick an account (7 to 10).
      2. Click Predict on the row above the chart. The card draws 5,000 possible markets for that account, following your plan.
      3. On the trend chart, the dashed curves show a good market (95th percentile), a middle one (median) and a poor one (5th percentile). The solid line is your plan.
      4. The Inflation line is your balance now raised by inflation. The histogram shows where the markets ended, and how many ended below it.
      5. To try another product or market outcome, click Change, pick it in Investment accounts, then click Predict again.
      What can’t the app answer yet?
      • CPP sharing between spouses (pension income splitting is modelled).
      • What happens when a spouse dies: survivor benefits and tax-free rollovers.
      • Whether your contributions fit your RRSP and TFSA room.
      • Your home and downsizing, LIRA and LIF accounts, and buying an annuity.
      • Spending is for comparison: a shortfall doesn’t take more from your accounts by itself.
      • Once you click Start planning, a setting such as the years to plan or inflation changes only through Save case & change settings.

      More in Reference: how the numbers are worked out (Help & Legal), “Main limitations”.

      The workflow

      Tab by tab (click a step to go to it):

      1. Cases & Settings
        1. You and your household
      2. Today’s Finances
        1. Spending
        2. Income
        3. Government pensions
        4. Investment contributions
        5. Investment accounts
      3. Retirement Planner
        1. Spending
        2. Income
        3. Investment contributions
        4. Investment balances
        5. Cash flow and tax
        6. Account balances and estate
      4. Cases & Settings
        1. Planned Cases
        2. Data download

      Each panel’s ?question-mark button explains it, and the User manual has the full guide. Text size (A, A+, A++), at the top right, makes the text larger. This is a learning tool, not financial or tax advice: please read the Disclaimer.

      Two ways to enter your numbers

      • Today’s Finances is a form. Type this year’s amounts in the boxes.
      • Retirement Planner does the same job on charts. Click a chart to add a point, and drag a point to change the amount in any year, not just this one.
      • The two stay in step. Change a number in one, and the other shows it.
      • A good way to start: fill in the form, then use the charts for changes in later years, such as a mortgage paid off.

      How investment account balances work

      • You enter balances, not withdrawals. In Investment accounts, type each account’s balance now.
      • To take money out, set a lower balance in a later year on the account’s chart in Investment balances, for example $0 in the plan’s last year.
      • The app works out the yearly withdrawal that gets there, rising with inflation. Growth follows the account’s product and its Outcome (Worst, Median or Best market).
      • A dotted line marks the years you contribute: nothing can come out then. The rest of the line is solid.
      • Some rules are built in: nothing is taken out while you still contribute to an account, and each RRIF pays at least its yearly minimum.
      • Or let the app do it: Plan withdrawals sets these balances for you (hollow circles on the charts).

      Investment products

      Picking a product for an account in Investment accounts copies its three numbers into that account; a plan keeps them even if you change the product later. Enter returns after fees. Built-in Growth, Balanced and Income are always here. Click a column heading to sort the table by it; click again to reverse.

      Default product for each account

      New plans start with these, for you and your spouse. Plans already set up keep their own.

      Planned Cases

      All amounts are in today’s dollars (inflation taken out), for the whole plan. Each account uses its selected outcome (Worst, Median or Best). Left to heirs: what your heirs would receive if you both died in the plan’s last year. Saved cases show their results as saved; the first row updates as you edit. Click a case’s row to load it; the pencil renames it and the × deletes it. Click a column’s heading to sort the saved cases by it, and click again to reverse; the arrow shows the order. They start sorted by Case, and a case just saved shows first until a heading is clicked. Download cases and Upload cases, beside the You, Spouse and Combined tabs, save the plan on screen and every case to a file and load it back. You and Spouse show each person’s own figures (and own estate); Combined stacks them, you solid and your spouse lighter.

      User manual

      Introduction

      Plan your retirement income, tax and estate year by year, for yourself or a couple, in any province or territory, using 2026 tax and benefit rules.

      Income it supports. Each kind has a fixed number, used on its row in the list, on the bars, in the legends and in the cards:

      • Your own income: 1 Employment income, 2 Pension and annuity, 3 Taxable interest, 4 Canadian dividends, 5 Other taxable income, 6 Non-taxable income.
      • Investment accounts: 7 Non-registered, 8 RRSP, 9 RRIF, 10 TFSA.
      • Government pensions: 11 CPP/QPP, 12 OAS.
      • Benefits the app works out for you: 13 GIS, 14 Allowance, 15 provincial top-up.

      Planning your income. Each year, the app adds up your income and account withdrawals, then takes off federal and provincial tax and any OAS clawback, to show what you keep. For your accounts, you set the balance you want in later years, and the app works out how much you can withdraw each year, tested over 5,000 simulated markets.

      Planning your spending. Your household’s costs come in six groups, such as Housing, Food and Travel and recreation. They start at what senior households like yours spend on average (Statistics Canada), so you only change what differs for you. Cash flow and tax shows them as orange bars beside what you keep, and a third bar for each year’s surplus or shortfall.

      Planning your savings. If you’re still saving, plan each person’s yearly contributions to the Non-registered account, RRSP and TFSA. They grow your balances, and nothing is withdrawn from an account while you contribute to it. They come out of after-tax income, so Cash flow and tax counts them as spending (purple bars under your costs). An RRSP contribution is deducted from that year’s income, which lowers your tax.

      Planning your estate. Each year, the app shows what your heirs would receive after tax and probate fees if you, your spouse, or both of you died that year.

      Help on each panel. The ?question-mark button at the right of a panel’s title opens a short card: what the panel is for, how to use it, and its notes (such as the inflation its lines rise with, or the RRSP’s last contribution year). This manual has the full guide.

      Seven tabs. The tabs at the top open one page at a time: first What, Why and How (what the app is, why you need it, how to make the most of it, Questions and answers in five groups (click a group’s name to show or hide its questions; the first shows at first), and Resources: government pages and Wikipedia articles on retirement), then, in the order of the work, Quick Start (the workflow; the app opens here), Investment Products (your list of investment products), Cases & Settings (Planned Cases, the planning settings with Start planning, and Data download), Today’s Finances (this year’s amounts), Retirement Planner (the charts, from Spending to Account balances and estate, with Plan withdrawals) and Help & Legal (this manual, the Reference, the Disclaimer and the License). Each page keeps its place when you come back to it. The left and right arrow keys move to the next or previous tab, except while you type in a box, choose from a list, work on a chart or have a window open. Undo and Redo, at the right of the tabs (or Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y), step back and forward through your changes to the plan, up to 100; loading a case, Start planning or an upload starts afresh. The browser’s Back and Forward buttons move between the tabs you’ve opened; with a window open (such as Plan’s card), Back closes it instead: only the top one, as Escape does.

      Text size. A, A+ and A++, at the top right, set the size of all the text, including the charts’; this browser remembers your choice. The page grows wider with the text, so on a large screen everything keeps its place on one row; on a smaller screen some rows wrap, your investment accounts and your spouse’s go one above the other, and on a narrow window the ages after Income’s and Contributions’ years make way (they are in each year box’s tooltip).

      This is a learning tool, not financial or tax advice. It works in whole years with simplified rules, so treat its numbers as estimates. Please read the Disclaimer, on this page.

      How to use the app

      1. Where you are today. Have at hand: recent account statements, the CPP Statement of Contributions (My Service Canada Account), pension statements and a recent pay stub. Then fill in:
        • You and your household, on the Cases & Settings tab. In the shaded row: Province or territory, Years to plan (5 to 30), the inflation to assume, Spouse or partner for a couple (without it, everything only for a spouse or the couple, such as the Spouse and Combined tabs, is hidden on every tab, and nothing else moves), and RRIF minimum by younger spouse’s age. Then, on a row for you and one for your spouse, the year of birth and the year Canadian residency began (the age and OAS years show after them), and, if you like, Plan to retire at: an age from next year’s to the one in the plan’s last year (its year shows after it). It draws a dashed line at that year on the charts and changes no numbers; leave it blank if you’ve retired or aren’t sure. Start planning is at its bottom right.
        • This year’s amounts, on the Today’s Finances tab, for you and your spouse, in five panels:
          • 1 Spending: this year’s amount for each of the six cost groups, per month or per year. They start at an estimated average from Statistics Canada data for a senior couple or a single senior; Use the averages puts them back.
          • 2 Income: this year’s employment income, taxable interest, Canadian dividends (the actual amount), other taxable and non-taxable income, and a pension’s yearly amount. Interest and dividends are for savings held outside the accounts you enter here. Employment income has a Through year after it, the last year it’s paid (first set to the year you turn 65), which works like the contributions’ Through. A pension has a From year after it, the first year it’s paid (first set to the year after employment income ends, or next year with none). The age shows after each year.
          • 3 Government pensions, per year in today’s dollars: the age CPP (QPP in Quebec) starts, the year that is, and the amount from then. Your Statement of Contributions (My Service Canada Account) gives estimates at different ages; change the age and the amount follows the CPP rules: 0.6% less for each month before 65, 0.7% more for each month after. Then the age OAS starts and the amount the app works out from your years in Canada after 18 and that age; if you already receive OAS, type the amount you get.
          • 4 Investment contributions: each account’s yearly amount, and Through after it, the last year you make it. “Through” starts at the last year of employment income. RRSP contributions stop by the year you turn 71, and an account takes no withdrawals while you contribute to it. Through is always a year you can type, even for a line shaped on its chart: an earlier year keeps the line’s shape to then and stops it; a later year carries the last year’s amount on to it.
          • 5 Investment accounts: each balance now, the product it holds (its capital gain, standard deviation and yield are on the Investment Products tab and in Investment balances, above the chart), the Market outcome, the market to plan on: Worst (only 1 market in 20 does worse), Median (the middle one) or Best (only 1 in 20 does better); and, for Non-registered, the Portfolio strategy: Hold all time (gains are taxed only on what you sell, and the rest when the last spouse dies) or Realize gains every year (gains and losses are taxed each year). From 1300 pixels wide (wider at a larger text size) you and your spouse sit side by side; on a narrower screen your spouse’s accounts are under yours.
        Amounts accept 125000, 125,000, $125K or 1.2M. Each panel’s arrow hides or shows it, and the last panel, This year’s totals, updates as you type. Start planning locks the settings (a padlock), opens the panels on Today’s Finances and the charts on Retirement Planner, and takes you to Today’s Finances; to change those settings, click Save case & change settings (in Cash flow and tax): your plan is saved, and a copy comes back with its settings open. Today’s Finances then stays open, in step with the charts: change an amount and its chart’s first point moves, and the reverse. A pension you reshape on its chart shows a dash instead of its From year; its amount box still sets this year’s point. After you click Start planning, the chart icon beside a row opens that row’s chart, on Retirement Planner.
      2. Spending, the first panel on Retirement Planner. Hover over a group to see what it covers. Click a group to shape its line over the years, per month or per year; Use the average puts it back. Each line rises with inflation. Everything else covers what the other groups don’t.
      3. Income. Pick You or Spouse, then a row in the list (1 to 6, 11 and 12), and shape its chart with points (see below). Each row shows its yearly amount in the year at the top of the list. You and Spouse here also switch Investment balances.
      4. Investment contributions. If you’re still saving, pick You or Spouse, then an account (7 Non-registered, 8 RRSP, 10 TFSA), and shape its contributions on its chart. Contributions start this year and end at the first $0 point; once they end, they can’t start again. RRSP contributions end in the year you turn 71. Each row shows the amount in the year at the top of the list, and the last contribution year. Leave them at $0 if you’ve stopped saving.
      5. Investment balances. Pick You or Spouse, then an account (7 Non-registered, 8 RRSP, 9 RRIF, 10 TFSA), and shape its balance with points (see below). Each row shows the balance at the end of the year at the top of the list. The line is dotted in the years you contribute, when nothing can come out, and solid in the others. Withdrawals can start the year after the last contribution.
      6. Read the results. Cash flow and tax shows up to three bars a year, side by side: gross income above $0 with tax below; net income above $0 with your spending below (household costs, then any contributions); and the surplus above $0, or the shortfall below. Spending and the surplus or shortfall are for the household, so they show on Combined (or You if you’re single). Tick the groups in its list to show one, some or all of them; Show income by source splits the income bar. Account balances and estate shows your balances and the estate after tax and probate; tick the accounts (7–10) and the estate in its list to show one, some or all of them. Show amounts in, under each list, draws the bars in each year’s dollars or in today’s dollars. Planned Cases, on Cases & Settings, shows lifetime totals in today’s dollars. You, Spouse and Combined choose whose numbers you see. Click or tap a year for its card with the exact amounts.
      7. Save and compare. Save case & change settings, at the bottom right of Cash flow and tax after Plan withdrawals, saves your plan as a case and opens Planned Cases with a copy of it on screen, its settings open to change; you can keep up to 30. The new case shows second, right under Case you’re working on. A plan that came from a case (one you loaded, or the copy Save brings back) is named “Updated” and that case’s name, such as Updated Case 4 (then Updated Case 4 (2), and so on); any other plan is named Case and its number. Saved cases are listed in Planned Cases, on Cases & Settings: click a case’s row to bring it back and keep editing (it opens with its settings open to change; click Start planning to work on its amounts and charts), the pencil to rename it, or the × to delete it. Click a column’s heading to sort the cases by it (again to reverse); they start sorted by Case. A case you’ve just saved shows first, under Case you’re working on, until you click a heading. When there’s a saved case, a flashing hint points to it: click a case to continue working on it. When all 30 are used, delete one before saving another.
      8. Keep your work. Cases last only until you close or reload the page; if you have cases or a plan of your own you haven’t downloaded, the browser asks before leaving (Back on the first tab you opened leaves the app too). In Planned Cases, Download cases saves the plan on screen and every case in one file, and Upload cases loads that file back (it replaces what’s on screen). A cases file must follow the app’s cases file template: the fields a downloaded file has, none missing and none added, each of the right kind (an account’s product name may be empty, and the list of Plan’s own points is there only when it has some). A file that doesn’t isn’t loaded, and nothing changes. Download data, in Data download (under the settings on Cases & Settings), gives your plan results as a spreadsheet (CSV); each row of the file is one year of one case. Pick the cases in Cases, then tick the panels to include (Spending, Income, Investment contributions, Investment balances, Cash flow and tax, Account balances and estate) and, in each one’s list, the details you want; Show amounts in chooses each year’s dollars or today’s. Each case is worked out with its own settings (each account’s outcome and strategy), as the app shows it. Always in the file: the case’s name and number, when it was saved, the year, ages, the household settings, and each account’s product and metrics (capital gain, standard deviation, yield, outcome and strategy).

      Working with data points

      Add
      Click or tap the chart above a year. A point appears on the line; drag it to the amount you want.
      Edit
      Drag a point: up or down changes the amount, left or right changes the year. For an exact amount, click the point, type it in the card’s Set amount (or Set balance) box, for example 125000, 125,000, $125K or 1.2M, and press Enter (Tab or a click elsewhere applies it too). If what you typed isn’t a number, nothing changes and the card says so. For a cost, first choose Per month or Per year. Holding the box’s arrows steps quickly.
      Delete
      Click the point, then Delete in its card.
      Note
      Click any point or marker (the CPP/OAS points too) and type in its card’s Note box, up to 512 bytes (about 500 letters; an accented letter counts 2, an emoji 4). It’s kept as you type, moves with its point and is deleted with it. A small note mark beside a point shows it has one. Notes are saved with the plan and its cases, and Download data lists them in its notes columns (spending, contributions, and income and accounts). Points you can’t change (a locked balance point, the RRSP’s age-71 point, the fixed CPP/OAS points, an OAS amount worked out for you and the CPP/OAS end mark) start with a default explanation of why, in italics and up to date with your plan. Edit it to make it your own note; clear it to bring the explanation back. A default explanation gets no mark and isn’t in the download.
      Keyboard
      Tab to a chart. The arrow keys move the selected point, Delete removes it and Escape lets it go.
      Read a year
      Move the pointer over any chart: a dashed cross shows the year, each person’s age and the dollar amount at the pointer, and the list beside the chart shows that year’s amounts. Click or tap to keep that year; it stays when you pick another row. In the list, ‹ and › step a year (hold one to step quickly); stepping back to this year, or Escape on the chart, lets the year go.
      • The first point (this year) and the end point move up or down only, and can’t be deleted. Between two points the line is straight: points a year apart make a sudden change, points further apart a gradual one.
      • CPP and OAS: drag the middle point left or right to choose the start year. Drag the last point up or down to your CPP amount; OAS is worked out from your years in Canada.
      • Accounts (Investment balances): the first point is your balance now. To take money out, add a lower point in a later year; the app works out the yearly withdrawal, rising with inflation, that gets there. The row above the chart shows the account’s Product, its capital gain, standard deviation and yield, its Market outcome and, for Non-registered, its strategy; they are set in Investment accounts, and Change takes you there, on the Today’s Finances tab. Predict shows the account’s plan in each of 5,000 possible markets, drawn in over about a second, with an Inflation line: your balance now raised by your inflation, the amount that keeps its buying power.
      • Plan: the button at the bottom right of Cash flow and tax plans the whole household’s withdrawals, and when CPP and OAS start.
        • The goal: the steadiest cash flow. Every retired year’s surplus (net income less spending and contributions, in today’s dollars) as close to one steady level as it can be, and each person’s net income steady too. The level comes from your own settings: what must come out anyway is spread evenly, and the rest stays invested. When your savings can’t keep up, the plan is a steady shortfall every year instead of running out at the end. Among plans equally steady, Plan keeps the one with the fewest jumps (in retirement, a year or three well above or below the years around it; while you work, any change, so CPP or OAS paid before work stops counts), then the one that leaves the least spending unpaid, then the most for you and your estate (your surplus plus the estate after tax). Tax isn’t compared on its own, so a steadier plan can pay a little more tax, as Demo cases 1 and 2 show.
        • What it tries: every CPP and OAS start age, a year at a time (CPP 60–70, or to 72 for QPP; OAS 65–70), for each of you, and ways of drawing: how much RRSP and RRIF income each of you takes before the other accounts (seven ceilings, one before and one after your CPP and OAS are both paid), the RRIF or Non-registered first or half each, and, before 65, sharing the draws so your incomes come out about the same. Hundreds of plans run on a quick model of the app; the best few are then worked out in full in the 5,000 markets. The card shows the best plan so far as it works, which can take a minute or two; Apply plan waits for the end, and Cancel stops it.
        • How it draws: from the year each person starts drawing (your first retired year, after work and RRSP contributions end), the RRSP moves to the RRIF each year only what’s drawn, so it’s RRIF income (pension income amount and splitting from 65) while the rest stays invested as the RRSP is, until 71. From 65 each person with a RRIF draws at least $2,000 a year from it, for the pension income amount. For a couple, the tax engine also splits eligible pension income between your returns each year.
        • Your points stay as they are: Plan adds points of its own (hollow circles) to the account lines only, never to income, spending or contributions, and an account with a point of yours later lands exactly on it. A plan that would move one of your points is dropped. Your RRSP stays as you set it if it, or your RRIF, has points of yours, or if its first year drawn follows a To RRIF % of yours below 100%. Click one of Plan’s points and Keep as mine makes it yours (so does moving it or changing its To RRIF %).
        • The retired years start when either of you stops working, or when the household’s income before withdrawals falls by 20% or more and stays down; before them Plan withdraws only to cover a shortfall.
        • Some years can still be off the level: above it when income alone, a RRIF minimum or one of your points brings more out; below it when the accounts Plan may use then are held by contributions or your points, or are empty. The card’s Why some years stand out names those years (numbered on its Cash flow chart), what changes in them, why Plan can’t even them out, and one or two things to try. An account still getting contributions isn’t drawn while it does, so ending them sooner lets Plan even out more.
        • The card shows five tiles (the steady level, the estate after tax, lifetime tax, and the CPP and OAS start ages, each against your plan now, in today’s dollars) and four charts, in today’s dollars or each year’s (Show amounts in; the steady level is in today’s dollars, so in each year’s it rises with your inflation): Cash flow (the household, or each of you), Account balances (with how often each runs short in the 5,000 markets; 5,000 markets draws them), CPP and OAS, and Estate after tax. Its ? explains them.
        • CPP and OAS start ages: a later start pays more for life but nothing until then, so it’s worth it only with a long life: the plan assumes you live to its end. To keep your own ages, untick Plan chooses CPP and OAS start ages on the card.
        • Nothing changes until Apply plan. Planning again replaces only Plan’s own points. If Plan finds nothing steadier than your plan now, the card says so and shows your plan now, and Apply plan stays off.
      • Investment products: a product is a name with its average annual capital gain, standard deviation and distribution yield (enter returns after fees). Your list is on the Investment Products tab (click it at the top, or Investment products… at the end of any Product list, opens it): add, edit, duplicate or delete products, and choose the product each account type starts with in a new plan; How to find a product’s numbers shows how. Click a column heading to sort the table by it, the built-in products too (again to reverse). Three built-in products are always there and can’t be changed: Built-in Growth (about 80% stocks, the most growth and the biggest swings), Built-in Balanced (about 60% stocks) and Built-in Income (about 30% stocks, paying out close to 4% a year, the smallest swings). Unless you choose others, a new plan starts Non-registered and RRSP accounts with Built-in Balanced, the RRIF with Built-in Income and the TFSA with Built-in Growth. Picking a product for an account copies its numbers into it; a plan keeps them if you change the product later (a small amber dot shows when they differ, and picking the product again uses the product’s numbers). An account whose file names no product shows Custom with its numbers until you pick a product. The list is kept in this browser; Download products saves it in a file, for another computer or to share with a team, and Upload products replaces the list with a file’s, after asking. A case or cases file that names a product your list doesn’t have adds it, with that account’s numbers.
      • RRSP and RRIF: each has its own row and chart (8 and 9). The RRSP reaches $0 in the year you turn 71, and what’s left moves to the RRIF. Each RRSP point’s To RRIF (%) sets how much of the money leaving the RRSP moves to the RRIF tax-free, from its year until the next RRSP point; the rest is taxable spending. The RRIF pays at least its yearly minimum from the year after money arrives.
      • Costs: a group’s line rises with inflation from this year’s amount. Add points where it changes: for a mortgage paid off in 2030, Housing with the payment in 2029 and without it in 2030.
      • Contributions: amounts are in each year’s dollars and stay level after the last point. Between points the line is straight, so to keep the full amount up to the year you stop, set a point at that amount in the year before the $0 point. Setting a point to $0 deletes the points after it.
      • Accounts you contribute to: on the balance chart, the contribution years (dotted) follow growth plus contributions, with no withdrawals and no points of your own. Withdrawals can start the year after the last contribution; your points after it work as usual. RRSP: To RRIF (%) is 100% in contribution years, and stays 100% after them until your next RRSP point. A plan saved by an earlier version of the app keeps the % it set for the years after the contributions; the card of the last contribution year says so.
      • Purple point: if a contribution change reaches years where you set balance points, those points are locked (faded) and the contribution point turns purple. Its card warns that any change to it will delete them; ending the contributions earlier unlocks them instead.
      • Amounts are in the dollars of each year, so future amounts include inflation. In Cash flow and tax, and in Account balances and estate, choose Today’s dollars under Show amounts in to draw the bars with inflation taken out.

      Reference: how the numbers are worked out

      For readers with a finance, investment or retirement-planning background. Rules and parameter values are as of 2026; in later years this version carries them forward with the inflation assumption and says so under the title, and each year’s new version brings that year’s rules. Amounts are nominal (each year’s dollars) unless stated otherwise.

      Conventions
      • Whole calendar years. The plan starts in the current year (2026) and runs for the chosen number of years. Cash flow and tax start in 2026; investment markets are simulated from 2027.
      • The inflation assumption indexes CPP/QPP, OAS, account withdrawals between points, tax brackets and credits, and benefit parameters from their 2026 values. Income lines you enter (employment, pension, interest, dividends, other, non-taxable) are nominal as entered.
      • Each source is modelled independently: no CPP or EI contributions on employment income, no interaction between sources other than through tax and benefits (and a couple’s pension income splitting, under Income tax).
      • Contributions are one line per person and account (Non-registered, RRSP, TFSA), in each year’s dollars as entered: straight between points, level after the last one. They start in the current year and stop for good at the first $0 point (the points after it are deleted); RRSP contributions stop after the year the owner turns 71. The last year with an amount above $0 is the last contribution year, L.
      • Household costs (Spending) are one list of six groups for the household. A group’s points are kept in today’s dollars and shown in each year’s dollars, raised by the inflation assumption: shown = point × (1 + inflation)^(year − 2026). Between points a cost changes along a straight line in today’s dollars; after the last point it stays level in today’s dollars.
      • Cost averages (estimates; a new plan starts at them, for a couple or a single person as Spouse or partner says, and Use the average puts a group back; a plan saved with its own amounts, including $0, keeps them), per month in 2026 dollars, senior couple / single senior: Housing $1,540 / $1,100; Food $970 / $540; Transportation $860 / $410; Health and personal care $470 / $250; Travel and recreation $620 / $270; Everything else $1,160 / $680; total $5,620 / $3,250. Method:
        • Statistics Canada’s Survey of Household Spending 2023, households whose reference person is 65 or over, average spending per household (table 11-10-0227-01). Housing is shelter, including mortgage payments, less travel lodging; air fares and travel lodging are in Travel and recreation (with recreation, education and reading); Health and personal care adds the two; Everything else is household operations (phone, internet, supplies, pets), furnishings, clothing, alcohol, tobacco and cannabis, games of chance and other spending. Income tax, pension and insurance contributions, and gifts are left out.
        • Each part is raised to 2026 by its own Consumer Price Index component, from the 2023 average to the January–August 2026 average (table 18-10-0004-01).
        • Couple and single: the survey has no table of seniors by household type, so each group is split with what one-person households spend relative to couples without children (table 11-10-0224-01; from 0.43 for Travel and recreation to 0.72 for Housing) and with about 4 in 10 senior households being one person (2021 Census, table 98-10-0134-01): couple = average ÷ (0.6 + 0.4 × ratio), single = couple × ratio, rounded to $10 a month.
        • Averages include households that spend nothing on an item (most senior households have no mortgage or rent), and they are national: no table splits senior spending by province.
      • Amounts on the screen are rounded for reading ($725, $8.1K, $450K; millions to the thousand, $14.523M; axis labels short, $20M); calculations use exact dollars, and the download rounds amounts to the whole dollar.
      Cash flow
      • What the chart shows: up to three bars a year, side by side, one for each group ticked in the list beside it, in this order. Gross income and tax: gross income (1–15) above $0, tax below $0. Net income and spending: net income above $0 (below $0 when tax is more than the cash received), household spending below $0 (household costs, then contributions). Surplus or shortfall: net income − household costs − contributions, above $0 in green or below $0 in red. Spending and the surplus or shortfall are household figures, so they show on Combined, or on You with no spouse. A group shown alone takes the whole width. Each row lists its parts this year for the view chosen. Show income by source draws each source and account with its ID. Show amounts in draws every bar, and the card, in each year’s dollars or in today’s dollars. The scale fits what is ticked, the legend lists only what the list doesn’t (sources, a tax refund, the spouse’s lighter shade), and a year’s card lists only the ticked groups. The choices are kept with the plan, its cases and the cases file.
      • On the chart and in its cards: Income (1–6, 11–15) = employment income, pension & annuity, taxable interest, Canadian dividends (the actual amount), other taxable income, non-taxable income, CPP/QPP, OAS before clawback, GIS, Allowance and provincial top-up. Investment (7–10) = Non-registered, RRSP spending, RRIF and TFSA withdrawals in full (Non-registered includes distributions paid out). Gross income (1–15) = Income + Investment. Tax = federal tax + provincial tax + recovery tax (OAS clawback) − any capital-loss carry-back refund. Amounts in the cards are exact dollars.
      • Taxable income = employment income, pension & annuity, taxable interest, other taxable income, CPP/QPP, OAS after clawback, RRSP spending, RRIF withdrawals, eligible dividends grossed up 38% (Canadian dividends, and the Non-registered account’s, paid out or reinvested) and 50% of the year’s realized capital gains. TFSA withdrawals and non-taxable income are excluded. GIS and the Allowance are in net income but deducted again, so they are never taxed (see Income tax).
      • Net income = Gross income + pension income split − Tax. The split is a couple’s pension income split (see Income tax), counted with the person who reports it, the money with its tax: plus for the one whose return reports it, minus for the one who splits it, and $0 in a year without one. All tax, including the tax on the Non-registered account’s dividends and realized gains, is paid from your cash, as you would with your tax return; the account pays out only your planned withdrawals. So net income can be below $0 in a year when the tax on reinvested income is more than the cash you receive; plan a withdrawal to cover it. In the CSV, each person’s Gross income, Pension income split on tax return and Total tax after refund columns reconcile to their Net income the same way (within $1 of rounding).
      • Combined adds both people; its card lists You, Spouse and the total. The two pension income split amounts cancel out, so the household’s net income = gross income − tax.
      • In a year with a capital-loss carry-back refund, the chart’s Tax is the total after the refund. A net refund (total tax below $0) is cash to you: it draws above $0 as a lighter Tax refund segment on the gross bar, and the card shows the Tax row as “+$… (refund)”. The download shows tax before the refund, the refund, and total tax after it (total = federal + provincial + recovery tax − refund), which can be a net refund.
      • Planned Cases: lifetime net income and tax are the household’s yearly amounts in today’s dollars, added up; total withdrawn adds every account withdrawal the same way; final investment balance and final estate are the last year’s (Combined estate), in today’s dollars. Up to 30 cases can be saved, each with a name you can change (up to 1,024 bytes; an accented letter counts 2). A saved case keeps the results it had when saved. When the page opens, four demo cases built into the app are already saved, each with notes on its points: a single 56-year-old in Ontario who plans to retire at 68, and a couple of 56 and 53 in British Columbia who plan to retire at 59 and 57, each before and after Plan withdrawals, so you can compare the two. They work like any other case, and uploading a cases file replaces them. You and Spouse show each person’s own amounts, with their own estate (as on that person’s view of Account balances and estate); Combined adds the two. Bars are scaled to the largest absolute value in their column for the view shown. The saved cases start sorted by name (the Case column, ascending, with its arrow showing). A column heading sorts them, ascending on the first click and reversing on each click after; the plan on screen stays first, names sort with their numbers in order (Case 2 before Case 10), amounts by the figure shown for the view, and ties keep case-number order. A case just saved with Save case & change settings shows first, right under the plan on screen, whatever the order, until a column heading is clicked; the table scrolls back to the top to show it. The order lasts until the page is reloaded.
      • Today’s dollars (under Show amounts in): amount in today’s dollars = amount ÷ (1 + inflation)^(year − 2026), for every bar and card amount; 2026 is the same either way.
      • Spending (on Combined, or on You with no spouse): household costs (orange) and, when the plan has any, contributions to the accounts (purple), each year. Contributions are paid from after-tax income, so they are spending too; the card lists each person’s by account. Surplus (or shortfall) = household net income − household costs − contributions; the third bar and the card show it when Surplus or shortfall is ticked. Costs are a comparison only: they change neither withdrawals nor tax. Contributions do change the plan: they add to the accounts, and an RRSP contribution is deducted from income (see Income tax). The download has each cost group, the household’s costs, contributions, spending and surplus in its Household columns, and each person’s contributions and RRSP deduction in their own columns.
      Income tax
      • Federal and provincial/territorial tax are calculated with the 2026 brackets, rates and credits of all 13 jurisdictions, per person on individual taxable income.
      • Non-refundable credits: basic personal amount, age amount (65+, income-tested), and the pension income amount (federal $2,000, plus provincial equivalents) on eligible pension income: Pension and annuity at any age; RRIF withdrawals from 65. Pension and annuity is for a workplace (registered) pension plan’s pension or life annuity; an annuity bought with RRSP money gets the credit only from 65, so before then enter it in Other taxable income.
      • Pension income splitting (couples, as Form T1032): each year the app moves up to half of a person’s eligible pension income onto the spouse’s return. That is Pension and annuity (taken as a pension plan’s life annuity) at any age, and RRIF withdrawals from the year the person turns 65. It picks the amount, either way, that gives the least income tax and OAS recovery tax on the two returns together. The receiving spouse’s pension income amount counts it from 65 (a pension plan’s annuity at any age). Quebec: Quebec’s own return allows a split only when the person splitting is 65 or older (line 245), with its own amount. So in Quebec the federal amount sets federal tax, the federal pension income amount and the OAS recovery tax, and a Quebec amount, chosen after it for the least Quebec tax ($0 while the person splitting is under 65), sets Quebec tax and its retirement income amount; the OAS repayment is deducted on both returns. Other provinces follow the federal amount. On a tax return no money moves, but in the cash flow the amount split counts with the person who reports it, the money with its tax: on You and Spouse it adds to that person’s net income and comes off the other’s (a part of the gross income and tax bar above $0 or below it), so each person’s net income matches their own return; the two cancel out on Combined. The year card shows it as Pension income split (in Quebec, a federal and a Quebec row when they differ; the cash follows the federal amount), Planned Cases and Data download’s Net_Income count it the same way, and Data download shows the amounts as Pension_Income_Split_on_Tax_Return (federal) and Pension_Income_Split_on_Provincial_Return. GIS, the Allowance and the provincial top-ups test the couple’s combined income, so the split doesn’t change them. RRSP withdrawals, CPP and OAS can’t be split; CPP sharing and a death year’s proration aren’t modelled.
      • Ontario surtax, Ontario Health Premium and Ontario tax reduction. Quebec: provincial tax, the 16.5% federal abatement, and the household-tested age and retirement-income credit. PEI, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick low-income reductions on family net income: one person’s amount for a single person, one each for a couple, with the same income threshold.
      • Future years: tax is computed on income deflated to 2026 dollars and scaled back by the inflation index.
      • The recovery tax (OAS clawback) is part of the year’s tax, and is deducted from that year’s income (line 23500). Canadian dividends (4) and Non-registered distributions are eligible Canadian dividends: grossed up 38% into income, with the federal dividend tax credit (15.0198% of the grossed-up amount) and the provincial one (Alberta 8.12%, BC 12%, Manitoba 8%, New Brunswick 14%, Newfoundland and Labrador 6.3%, Nova Scotia 8.85%, Northwest Territories 11.5%, Nunavut 5.51%, Ontario 10%, PEI 10.5%, Quebec 11.7%, Saskatchewan 11%, Yukon 12.02%). Both credits are non-refundable. Capital gains inclusion rate 50%.
      • Net income vs taxable income. Net income (line 23600) includes grossed-up dividends and taxable capital gains, and the GIS and Allowance paid that year (line 14600), less the recovery tax. The recovery tax, the age amount, the household reductions, the NL Seniors’ Benefit and Quebec’s senior assistance use it. GIS and the Allowance use their own income test, which leaves out OAS, GIS and the Allowance (grossed-up dividends count at 138% for all of them). Taxable income = net income − GIS and Allowance not taken back by the recovery tax (line 25000) − net capital losses of other years; it sets the tax brackets.
      • RRSP deduction. Each year’s RRSP contribution is deducted from that year’s income (as on line 20800), up to the income, so net income and taxable income are both after it, and so are the age amount, the OAS clawback, GIS, the Allowance, provincial top-ups and household reductions. A deduction larger than the year’s income isn’t carried forward, and contribution room isn’t checked.
      CPP and QPP
      • The user enters the yearly amount at the chosen start (for example from the Service Canada or Retraite Québec statement). It is stored as the age-65 equivalent in today’s (2026) dollars, so moving the start re-applies the adjustment.
      • Start age 60–70 (QPP: 60–72 when the province is Quebec), whole years. Adjustment: −0.6% per month before 65 (−36% at 60); +0.7% per month after 65 (+42% at 70; QPP +58.8% at 72). QPP’s early reduction uses CPP’s 0.6% rate, a conservative simplification.
      • 2026 maximum at 65: $1,507.65 a month. Indexed yearly by the inflation assumption. For existing recipients, the entered current-year amount is indexed forward.
      OAS and the recovery tax (clawback)
      • Maximum $751.97 a month at 65–74; +10% from 75.
      • Benefit rates: OAS, GIS and the Allowance all use the July–September 2026 rates for the whole of 2026, then rise with the inflation setting. So each year’s amount is a year of those rates, not the exact payments, which change every quarter.
      • Residence share = min(years in Canada after 18, 40) ÷ 40, with at least 10 years. Earliest start = the later of 65 and the age at which 10 years are reached; latest start = earliest + 5 years.
      • Deferral: +0.6% per month after first eligibility (up to +36%). The app uses the higher of (a) the residence share at the start age with no deferral increase and (b) the share at first eligibility × (1 + deferral increase), since both can’t apply to the same months.
      • Existing recipients default to an estimate: OAS as if started at first eligibility, with no deferral increase. The user can replace it with the actual amount.
      • Recovery tax for income year y: rt(y) = min(OAS(y) + GIS(y) + Allowance(y), 15% × (income(y) − $95,323 × index)), where income (line 23400) includes OAS, the GIS and Allowance paid that year and all taxable sources, less the RRSP deduction. It takes back OAS first, then GIS and the Allowance (CRA’s worksheet); what is left of GIS and the Allowance is deducted for taxable income (line 25000). It is assessed on that year’s return, so it is part of that year’s tax, and its deduction comes off that year’s income (line 23500). The app works in whole years: what is withheld from later OAS payments, and refunded or settled when filing, is timing only and is left out.
      GIS, the Allowance and provincial top-ups
      • Income test: combined taxable income of the couple excluding OAS, with employment income reduced by the earnings exemption (the first $5,000, plus 50% of the next $10,000), less RRSP deductions. EI benefits get no exemption, so enter them as other taxable income. TFSA and non-taxable income are excluded.
      • Timing: payment year Y uses 0.5·benefit(income Y−1) + 0.5·benefit(income Y−2); earlier years use the first plan year. Eligibility (OAS in pay, ages) is as of year Y. All parameters are July–September 2026 values, indexed. The provincial top-ups follow the same timing (they are paid July to June from the previous year’s income), except Quebec’s senior assistance: a credit on each year’s return, from that year’s family net income.
      • Single: up to $1,123.17 a month. The base part falls 50¢ per $1 of income; the top-up part ($173.67) falls 25¢ per $1 above $2,016; nil at $22,800.
      • Couple, both receiving OAS: Service Canada’s couple rates (up to $676.09 a month each), per person on combined income. Partner not receiving OAS or the Allowance: Service Canada’s higher rate for this situation (up to $1,123.17 a month), on combined income.
      • Allowance (age 60–64, partner receives OAS, 10+ years’ residence): up to $1,428.06 a month, which is $751.97 (OAS-equivalent) + $676.09 (couple GIS). The OAS-equivalent part falls 75¢ per $1 of combined income; above $12,031.52 the GIS-equivalent part and the partner’s GIS follow the couple scale on the excess; nil at $42,144.
      • Provincial senior top-ups (2026 benefit-year figures; single or couple as Spouse or partner sets):
        • Ontario GAINS: up to $92 a month each. Single: less 25¢ per $1 of GIS income (nil at $4,416). Couple: each less 12.5¢ per $1 of combined income (nil at $8,832).
        • Quebec senior assistance (70+, 2026 figures): $2,000 each, less 5.47% of that year’s family net income over $28,405 (single) or $46,200 (couple; shared when both are 70+).
        • Alberta Seniors Benefit (homeowner, renter or lodge resident): single up to $3,946 a year, less 0.1714 per $1; couple up to $5,918, less 0.1717 per $1 of combined income, split equally when both receive OAS. Income is total income less OAS, the RRSP deduction and up to $3,600 of employment income.
        • BC Senior’s Supplement: up to $99.30 a month (single) or $110.25 each (couple), in proportion to GIS.
        • Manitoba 55 PLUS (55+): single up to $161.80 a quarter (nil at $9,746.40); couple up to $173.90 each a quarter (nil at $16,255.20 of family income). A straight-line approximation of the program’s tables.
        • NL Seniors’ Benefit (65+): one benefit per family, up to $1,882 a year, less 11.66% of family net income (GIS and the Allowance included) over $30,409; shared when both spouses qualify.
        • Northwest Territories and Nunavut: a flat monthly supplement for GIS recipients from 60.
      • Partial OAS: a pensioner with fewer than 40 years in Canada after 18 gets extra GIS equal to the OAS they don’t receive: $751.97 × 12 × (1 − residence share), before any deferral increase and without the 10% at 75. It is paid in full until the ordinary GIS runs out, then falls by 50¢ per $1 of income (single) or 25¢ each (couple). OAS plus GIS then match a full-pension pensioner at the same income. The Allowance is not prorated for residence.
      • GIS, the Allowance and top-ups are not taxed. GIS and the Allowance still count in net income, so they lower the income-tested programs and credits that use it, and the recovery tax can take them back in a high-income year.
      The setup panels and investment products
      • What the boxes write: each amount is its chart’s first point (this year; spending in today’s dollars). Employment income: the amount to its Through year (first the year you turn 65), then a $0 point the year after (none when that is the plan’s last year). A pension: $0 points until the year before it starts, then the amount. A contribution: the amount to its Through year, then a $0 point (the RRSP stops by the year its owner turns 71). CPP/QPP: the start age, and the amount from it in today’s dollars, kept as the amount at 65 (the amount divided by the start age’s adjustment); OAS: the start age, and the amount you get if you already receive it. The same rules apply as on the charts, so a plan entered here is the plan you’d get by setting the same points on the charts.
      • Reading it back: a pension line still in its shape shows its From year; any other shape (points added on its chart) shows a dash instead, and its amount box changes only this year’s point. Employment income and each contribution always show their Through year, the last year with an amount (contributions can’t restart; a break in employment income counts only its last year). Typing an earlier year keeps a shaped line as it is up to that year, with a point on the line there, and adds a $0 point the year after. A later year carries the last year’s amount on to it. A line still in the simple shape is written as above. First guesses: a pension from the year after employment income ends (next year with none), contributions through the last year of employment income. While an amount is $0, its year box is greyed and shows the year it will start with.
      • Accounts: each account’s product (its three numbers are on the Investment Products tab), Outcome and, for Non-registered, portfolio management strategy are set in Investment accounts; the account row in Investment balances shows them (display only). From 1300 px (wider at a larger text size) the two people sit side by side; below that, one above the other.
      • Products: a name (up to 60 characters, each different), average annual capital gain (0–35%), standard deviation (0–40%) and distribution yield (0–20%), to two decimals, and a note (up to 200 characters). The list holds up to 100 of your own (Add product stops there); names must be different, and names starting “Built-in” are kept for the app. Each account type’s default is the one chosen on the Investment Products tab, else the app’s: Built-in Balanced (Non-registered, RRSP), Built-in Income (RRIF), Built-in Growth (TFSA). An account keeps the numbers and name it was given; it shows Custom when it has no product name, and an amber dot when its numbers differ from the product of the same name.
      • Built-in Growth, Balanced and Income (capital gain / standard deviation / yield): 8.88 / 10.52 / 1.74, based on Vanguard Growth ETF Portfolio (VGRO, about 80% stocks and 20% bonds, January 2018 to August 2026); 6.13 / 8.71 / 2.11, Vanguard Balanced ETF Portfolio (VBAL, about 60/40, same period); 1.95 / 6.94 / 3.85, Vanguard Retirement Income ETF Portfolio (VRIF, about 30/70 with a monthly payout near 4% a year, September 2020 to August 2026). Method: standard deviation of monthly total returns since inception, annualized; capital gain = the yearly total return since inception after fees (Vanguard Canada fact sheets and ETF Facts, 31 August 2026) plus half the variance, the average the market model uses, less the yield; yield = the 12-month trailing distribution yield at 30 September 2026. Vanguard’s family was chosen over iShares and BMO for its longer history and one method for all three. The history is short and mostly strong; FP Canada’s 2026 Projection Assumption Guidelines imply lower capital gains (about 4.47 / 3.28 / 0.28). They are in every browser, can’t be changed, aren’t written to products files, and names starting “Built-in” are kept for the app (a product of your own saved earlier under such a name is kept as “My …”).
      • Where products are kept: your products and each account type’s default are saved in this browser (its local storage) at every change, so they’re there the next time you open the app here; another browser or computer has its own list (use Download products and Upload products to move it). A private window, or blocked or cleared site data, keeps nothing: then Not saved in this browser shows beside the title on the Investment Products tab, and the list lasts until the page closes. A saved list that can’t be read in full keeps every product that can, the page says what was left out, and the saved text is kept as it was (Download the saved copy). Chrome and Edge share it between the app’s files on this computer. The products file (Download products) is JSON with the products and each account type’s default, and no version; Upload products checks it against the products file template and its values, and replaces the list only after you confirm.
      • Cases files: each account has a product field (empty when none). A file without it loads, and its accounts keep their numbers. A loaded plan or case naming a product your list doesn’t have adds it, with that account’s numbers. An account can also have a planned list: the years of Plan’s own points on its line, written only when there are some. A file without it loads with every point counted as yours; a year with no point is dropped.
      Investment accounts: growth and withdrawals
      • Points are year-end balances; the first point is the current balance. The Account balances and estate chart and the download use true year-end balances: for the current year, the balance now minus the RRIF minimum. The download also gives each year’s opening balance (the previous year-end), so opening + growth − withdrawal = year-end on every row.
      • Current year (no market simulation): prices don’t move, but every account earns its distribution yield on the balance now, which is reinvested; the RRIF minimum (on the January 1 balance) comes out; the tax on the Non-registered dividend is paid from your cash; no planned withdrawals.
      • From next year: 5,000 simulated paths from a fixed seed (mulberry32 generator, Box–Muller normals). Each path’s yearly price factor is lognormal with mean m = 1 + capital gain and standard deviation s: σ² = ln(1 + s²/m²), μ = ln m − σ²/2. Growth factor = price factor + distribution yield d. Year-end update: B(t) = max(0, B(t−1)·(f(t) + d) − W(t)). All accounts share the same simulated market years.
      • Between points a < b, withdrawals rise with inflation: W(t) = W·(1 + i)^(t−a−1). W is the value at which the selected percentile of ending balances equals the point. Each path carries its own balance from one point to the next (nothing restarts at a point), so B(a) is that path’s balance, and adding a point where the line already is changes nothing after it. For Non-registered, TFSA and RRSP this is exact: each path gives W = (B(a)·A − B(b)) ÷ C, with A the product of growth factors and C the inflation-weighted compounding of withdrawals, and W is that percentile across paths. RRIF: each path withdraws max(W(t), minimum), solved by a bracketed secant search. A $0 point empties every path, so the account stays at $0 after it in every market.
      • The line shows the selected percentile of balances each year; points are shown exactly. Each year’s piece of the line (from the previous year end) is dotted in contribution years (up to L, below; an RRSP maturing in a contribution year included) and solid in every other year. “Highest possible” for a point = the selected percentile with no withdrawals (RRIF: minimum only) from the paths’ balances at the previous point; higher points are lowered when saved. After the last point there are no planned withdrawals.
      • No account ever pays out more than it holds: when a selected outcome runs an account down to $0, each of the 5,000 market paths pays the planned amount or what that path still holds, whichever is less, and that year’s withdrawal is the selected percentile of those payments. The card then shows both the planned and the paid amount. In the year an RRSP matures, each path pays out everything it holds, and what leaves the RRSP (split by its To RRIF %) is the selected percentile of those amounts. A RRIF minimum it can’t cover is shown in its card as “Minimum not covered”.
      • RRSP: drawn down gradually to $0 by December 31 of the year its owner turns 71 (a fixed endpoint; whatever is left that year leaves); between points the outflow rises with inflation. Each point’s To RRIF % splits the outflow, until the next point, into a tax-free direct transfer to the RRIF and taxable spending, which does not qualify for the pension income amount. RRIF: transfers arriving during a year are available for that year’s withdrawal and are included when solving for a balance target; the minimum is on the January 1 balance, so a RRIF funded by a transfer has no minimum until the following year. The RRIF uses the transfers of the RRSP outcome shown. Minimum factor 1/(90 − age) below 71; prescribed factors from 71 (5.28%) to 94 (18.79%); 20% from 95; age on January 1; younger-spouse election available. Withdrawals are fully taxable and qualify for the pension income amount from 65.
