      • Contributions are added at the end of each year they are made, after that year’s growth, in every path: B(t) = B(t−1)·(f(t) + d) + C(t), with no withdrawal; in the current year, year-end = balance now × (1 + d) + C. Up to the last contribution year L, the line is the selected percentile of balances with contributions. The balance at L acts as a point, though none is drawn there: the paths carry on from it with their own balances, withdrawals between it and your next point are solved as above, and a later point can be no higher than that balance can grow to. With no later point, the account grows with no withdrawals.
      • Your balance points in contribution years (after the current year, up to L) are locked: shown faded and not used. The contribution point whose edit locked them turns purple; the next change to its value or year deletes them, while an edit that ends the overlap unlocks them.
      • RRSP contributions: the To RRIF % is 100% up to L (the only outflow then is the age-71 maturity, which moves wholly to the RRIF); after L, it stays 100% until your next RRSP point. Non-registered contributions add to the cost base and are never a gain: under Hold they buy units at cost. TFSA contributions aren’t deducted and grow tax-free.
      • Non-registered has two portfolio management strategies, chosen per person (Portfolio strategy in Investment accounts; a new plan starts with Hold all time). Realize gains every year is described next. Hold all time: dividends are taxed the same way, but gains are realized only on units sold, at average cost (gain = amount sold − cost base × amount sold ÷ unit value); reinvested dividends add to the cost base; the unsold gain grows untaxed until the last survivor dies (see Estate). A sale below the cost base realizes a loss, handled as below.
      • Realize gains every year: both parts of the return are realized and taxed, withdrawn or not. The distribution (yield × January 1 balance) is an eligible Canadian dividend; the year’s price change close + withdrawal − opening − dividend − contribution is a realized capital gain (half taxable) or loss. So no gain builds up untaxed, and the cost base always equals the balance. The withdrawal is paid from the dividend first, then the year’s gain, then capital; the rest is reinvested. In the current year prices don’t move, so there is no gain; the dividend is reinvested.
      • Tax on investment income is paid from your cash. As in real life, the tax on the Non-registered account’s dividends and realized gains is paid with your tax return (or by instalments or extra withholding), from your cash, not from the account. It is part of each year’s Tax in Cash flow and tax, so it comes out of net income; the account pays out only your planned withdrawals and reinvests the rest. Under Hold, units are sold only for withdrawals (the dividend is used first; never more than exist), and a dividend left over is reinvested at cost; a fully sold account ends with no units, value or cost base. Each account is worked out once, so results are exact. For information, the account’s point card and the download show the tax its income adds to your return (an estimate: tax(other income + grossed-up dividends + taxable gains − carried losses) − tax(other income), with the dividend tax credit; a carried-back loss can make it a saving). The estimate counts the year’s GIS and Allowance as paid in net income for the credits, as your return does. It leaves out the recovery tax, any change in benefits and, for a couple, your spouse’s Non-registered income in shared credits, so it can differ a little from the change in your total Tax. If you would rather sell units to pay that tax, lower that year’s balance point to plan the withdrawal.
      • Capital losses: half of a year’s loss is an allowable loss. It can’t reduce dividends, employment or other income. Unused, it is carried back up to three years to taxable gains of those plan years (earliest first), then forward with no time limit. Carried losses reduce taxable income only, so they don’t change the OAS clawback or GIS. A carry-back amends the earlier return: that year’s tax stays as filed, and the refund (earlier tax minus amended tax) is paid in the loss year. It lowers that year’s Tax in Cash flow and tax, is cash to you, and isn’t reinvested in the account. The download shows it as Capital_Loss_Carry_Back_Refund. Realizing a loss while staying invested assumes a similar but not identical investment is bought, since CRA denies a loss when the same property is bought back within 30 days (superficial loss).
      • TFSA: withdrawals are tax-free and excluded from the benefit and clawback income tests. Contribution room isn’t checked (the 2026 limit is $7,000 a year, and unused room carries forward).
      Plan: the household’s withdrawals
      • What it does: sets the household’s withdrawals, and the CPP and OAS start ages, for the steadiest cash flow: every retired year’s surplus, net income − household costs − contributions in today’s dollars, as close to one steady level as it can be. It changes only its own points (on the account lines, including the RRSP’s move to the RRIF and its To RRIF %) and the start ages when it picks others. Your points (with their To RRIF %s and notes), products, outcomes, strategies, income, spending, contributions, CPP amounts and this year’s balances stay as they are.
      • The level comes from your settings alone: the lowest level that is steadiest, at least a $1,000 cushion. Plan starts at the cushion and raises the level while years are above it, from what must come out (RRIF minimums, the pension income amount, your points) or from income alone (a block of later years with CPP, OAS or a pension), spread over the retired years, as long as each step makes the years steadier, and never above the highest level the accounts can keep up. A single year above it (a last year of part-time work) hardly moves it. When the savings can’t keep even the cushion, the level is the highest they can keep up: a steady shortfall every year instead of running out at the end. The card also shows the highest level the accounts could keep up with the plan’s ages and way of drawing, in whole hundreds: found on the quick model (below) and checked on the engine, leaving no more spending unpaid than the plan’s own level.
      • How plans compare: the steadiest first: the average gap over the retired years between each year’s surplus and the level, plus, for a couple, half of each person’s average gap from their own average net income (a pension income split counted with the one who reports it). Plans within $500 a year of each other count as equally steady; among them, the fewest jumps (within $500 in all), each beyond $250 a year, added up. In the working years, each change from the year before: a start age that pays out while you still work makes a step up, then a bigger fall when work stops. In the retired years, each year’s distance from the middle value of the seven years around it (fewer at the ends), so a spike of one to three years counts but a lasting step (a pension that stays) doesn’t. The quick model (below) counts only the working years; the plans worked out in full count both. Then the least spending left unpaid (within $1,000 over the plan), then the most for you and your estate: every year’s surplus plus the after-tax estate at the plan’s end (both of you dying in the last year, after tax and probate, as Planned Cases shows it). Tax and clawback aren’t compared on their own, so a steadier plan can pay a little more tax. A plan is offered only if it beats your plan now, both compared the same way: each one’s gap from its own average over the retired years, every year counted, then its jumps. If none does, the card says Plan found nothing steadier than your plan now, shows your plan now and the highest steady surplus your savings could keep up (on Plan’s best plan), and Apply plan stays off.
      • Ways of drawing: each year, first what must come out: RRIF minimums; from 65, at least $2,000 a year (2026 dollars, indexed) of RRIF for each person while it has money, for the pension income amount; and what lands an account on your point that year. Then, by the way of drawing: each person’s RRIF and then their RRSP through it (below), together up to their room under a ceiling, ceiling × indexation − income before the RRIF (their taxable sources and OAS, less the RRSP deduction, before any pension split), and Non-registered, in the order chosen; then the TFSA; then the RRIF and RRSP above the ceiling. The ceiling is half the top of the first federal bracket, its top ($58,523), halfway to the OAS clawback line, the line ($95,323), halfway to the top of the second bracket, its top ($117,045), or none, in 2026 dollars: one until both a person’s CPP and OAS are paid, another from then. The order is the RRIF first, Non-registered first, or half each. Shared (a couple, while either is under 65): the RRIF draws go first to whoever has the lower income before them, so both incomes come out about the same; otherwise each account gives in proportion to what it can. From 65 the $2,000 for the pension income amount comes through the RRIF from the RRSP when the RRIF itself holds less. An account still receiving contributions gives nothing until they stop.
      • The search: on a quick model of the app, every CPP and OAS start age, a year at a time, one benefit at a time, from your ages, all the earliest, all the latest and all the middle ones, until no single change does better; then, for the three best sets of ages, every ceiling (before and after), order and sharing, one setting at a time; then the best ages again with the best way of drawing. Each plan tried gets its own level. The quick model runs each account along its Outcome in one market (the chosen percentile of the 5,000 markets’ growth, the yield included), with the same withdrawal rules and the same tax, OAS recovery tax and best pension income split each year; GIS and provincial top-ups stay as on screen. The four best plans that differ are then solved on the engine, each at its own level (moved while that helps), and the best is kept. The card says how many plans were tried.
      • RRSP: each person’s RRSP is drawn through the RRIF from the year they start drawing: the first retired year, after their employment income and RRSP contributions end. A point of Plan’s keeps it whole to the year before (its highest possible). From then on, each year the RRSP moves to the RRIF only what Plan draws from it (points of Plan’s, To RRIF 100%), and the RRIF pays it out the same year: it’s RRIF income, with the pension income amount and pension splitting from 65, which RRSP withdrawals don’t get. The rest stays in the RRSP, invested as you set it (its product), until it matures in the year its owner turns 71, when what’s left moves to the RRIF (at that point’s To RRIF %) and is invested as the RRIF from then on. In real life that’s a transfer each year, or converting it all and keeping the same investments. A RRIF that only passes money on stays near $0, so its minimums stay small. The RRSP stays as you set it when it or the RRIF has points of yours (your RRIF points are shaped on what the RRSP moves in), when its first year drawn follows a To RRIF % of yours below 100% (Plan never changes yours), and when it matures at 71 before the drawing starts.
      • Pension income splitting for a couple is part of the tax engine (see Income tax), so every plan, Plan’s included, has it. On You and Spouse, the amount split counts with the person who reports it, the money with its tax.
      • Your points and Plan’s: every point you set is yours. Plan’s are listed in the account’s planned list (saved in cases files) and drawn as hollow circles; a new plan replaces only them. Moving one of Plan’s points, changing its To RRIF %, giving it a note, or Keep as mine on its card makes it yours. A plan that would show one of your points lower on the chart (out of reach) is dropped for the next best; if every one would, Plan keeps your plan and says so.
      • Retired years: from the first year either person has no employment income, or the first year the household’s income before withdrawals (work, pensions, CPP, OAS, interest, dividends, other and non-taxable income, in today’s dollars) is 20% or more below the median of the up to three years before it and stays there the next year, whichever comes first; next year when neither works. Before them, Plan withdraws only to lift a year that would fall short to $0.
      • Stretches: each account starts at your last point before the retired years (or this year’s balance). Up to each later point of yours it is a stretch: each year Plan takes at most what still lets the account reach that point, and in the point’s year exactly what lands on it. In the retired years a stretch also draws at least the level amount (rising with inflation, as the engine draws between points) that lands on the point, so the money doesn’t build up and come out in one taxed lump. In a year that needs less because of extra income not from work (a one-off amount, say), the level amount gives way, when the point is three years off or more, up to one year’s level amount on the stretch in all; what stays is spread over the years left. A year either of you still works is part of retiring, a step down rather than a jump, and keeps the level amount. After your last point the account is free.
      • Years off the level: above it when income alone, a RRIF minimum, the $2,000 floor or one of your points brings more out. When later years stay well above it after years at it, something keeps money from the years before: an account that still gets contributions (none is drawn while it does) or your points. A year below it is one whose gap is more than the accounts Plan may use then could pay even with nothing taken before it (one still gets contributions, or your points keep money for later), or whose accounts are empty. Plan leaves it short instead of lowering every other year.
      • Why some years stand out (on the card, under Cash flow): up to four years, the biggest, numbered on the chart. Runs of retired years off the level (above it only from $2,000 or a fifth of the level, whichever is more); then one to three other years above or below the years either side of them (measured against those not explained already, so years between two bigger dips don’t count); then working years that fall short. Well off is the largest of $1,000, three times the plan’s usual change from one year to the next, and 3% of a year’s spending. For each: what changes most that year (a year off the level is compared with a year at it), why Plan can’t even it out, and one or two things to try in the app. With your plan kept (nothing steadier), it explains your plan’s jumps. A red note names a point of yours Plan couldn’t keep within reach.
      • CPP and OAS start ages: Plan may choose each person’s CPP (QPP) start age, when they have a CPP amount, and OAS start age, when either hasn’t started: not already receiving it, and under the latest start. CPP from 60 to 70 (72 for QPP), OAS from first eligible (usually 65) to five years later, each from next year at the soonest and not past the plan’s end. Apply plan sets them in Government pensions and on the charts. With Plan chooses CPP and OAS start ages unticked (on the card, not saved), your ages stay. The plan assumes both of you live to its end.
      • How it’s solved: on the engine, each year’s withdrawals are run through the account’s 5,000 markets, and the selected percentile of the balances after them becomes that year’s point; with a point every year, the engine’s own solver gives back exactly that withdrawal (Plan hands it each year’s withdrawal as its first try, which it checks, so it rarely needs to search). The full engine (tax, pension splitting, OAS clawback, GIS, capital gains) then gives each year’s surplus, and each year’s withdrawal is corrected by its gap, grossed up for the tax it adds (estimated from the last two runs), until every year is within about $50.
      • Fewest points: from each point, the longest stretch is kept, ending at most at your next point, whose single withdrawal (rising with inflation, as the engine draws between points) is within $600 in today’s dollars of each year’s withdrawal; Plan’s points are rounded to the hundred (a stretch with nothing drawn ends at the account’s highest, in whole dollars, so nothing trickles out), yours stay exact. A stretch in which the account would run dry before its end while more is still planned isn’t kept, so the 5,000-market view never shows a planned withdrawal the account can’t pay. While solving, Plan’s points are exact (not rounded), so the engine follows Plan’s withdrawals exactly. An account where that would leave one of your points out of reach keeps a point every year, as solved. The engine checks that no year’s surplus moves by more than $850, and otherwise tries again with half the margin (or keeps a point every year).
      • Short in N% of markets: the red tag on an account’s chart: the share of the 5,000 markets in which the account can’t pay the planned withdrawal (or the RRIF minimum) in some year, from the same replay as the 5,000-market view (5,000 markets draws them). At Median about half of markets do worse than the plan, so an account planned to run down runs out sooner in them; Worst is the cautious choice.
      • The card opens at once with the plan now, then shows the best plan found so far as Plan works (on the quick model, then on the engine, so the figures settle at the end); Apply plan waits for the end. It has five tiles (the steady level, with the highest the accounts could keep up and the plan now’s range; the estate after tax; lifetime tax; the CPP and OAS start ages; each against the plan now) (in today’s dollars) and four charts, Plan solid and the plan now dashed, in today’s dollars or each year’s (Show amounts in; the steady level rises with inflation in each year’s): Cash flow (the household’s surplus with the level, or each person’s net income), Account balances (each account at year end, the RRSP and RRIF together, your points filled and Plan’s hollow), CPP and OAS (each person’s, stacked) and Estate after tax (both of you, or each of you, dying that year). Its ? explains it.
      • Which points are Plan’s is saved in cases files.
      How the account types compare

      Non-registered, RRSP, RRIF and TFSA use the same engine: the same points, the same market simulation (price change plus distribution yield), the same Worst, Median and Best outcomes, and the same current-year pause. They differ only in tax: while the money is invested, and when it comes out.

      Non-registeredRRSP / RRIFTFSA
      ContributionsFrom after-tax cash; added to the cost baseRRSP only, up to the year you turn 71; deducted from that year’s incomeFrom after-tax cash; not deducted
      Distributions and gains while investedEligible dividends taxed every year (grossed up 38%, with dividend tax credits). Gains: taxed every year (Realize), or only on units sold (Hold)Reinvested, not taxedReinvested, not taxed
      Market lossesAllowable capital losses when realized (every year, or on a sale below cost): carried back 3 years, then forwardNo tax effectNo tax effect
      WithdrawalsPaid from the dividend first. Realize: then the year’s gain, then capital. Hold: then unit sales, each part gain and part costFully taxable as ordinary income, however the money grew (no dividend credit, no half-taxed gains)Tax-free
      Counted for the OAS clawback, GIS and the AllowanceGrossed-up dividends and taxable gains, every yearThe whole withdrawalNever
      Required withdrawalsNoneThe RRIF minimum every yearNone
      Who pays the tax on the account’s incomeYou, every year, from your cash (with your tax return)You, when money is withdrawnNo tax
      Pension income amountNoYes, from 65No
      At the last survivor’s deathUnsold gains taxed as if sold, half taxable (Hold only)The whole balance taxed as incomeTax-free
      Current year (the pause)Prices don’t move; the dividend is reinvested and its tax paid from your cashPrices don’t move; the yield is reinvested; the RRIF minimum comes outPrices don’t move; the yield is reinvested

      For RRSP / RRIF, growth is untaxed only while it stays in the account: a dollar of growth that would be half-taxed as a capital gain in a Non-registered account is fully taxed as income when it comes out of the RRSP or RRIF as spending. That is the other side of the deduction received when the money was contributed. The TFSA is the only account whose growth is never taxed. Contributions to all three count as spending in Cash flow and tax; only the RRSP’s are deducted.

      Estate
      • The Estate bar answers: what would heirs receive, after tax, if a person died at the end of this year? You: your own accounts, as if you had no spouse to inherit tax-free. Spouse: your spouse’s own accounts, as a surviving spouse (no further tax-free rollover). Combined: you both die that year, each estate on its own final return, added together (the spouse’s part stacked, lighter). Credits that depend on household income (Quebec’s age and retirement credit; the PEI, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick low-income reductions) then see the other person’s income on their final return, so Combined can be a little less than You plus Spouse.
      • On a final return, the whole RRSP and RRIF balance is income, and unsold Non-registered gains are deemed realized (half taxable); under Realize gains every year there are none. The TFSA passes tax-free.
      • Tax at death compares two returns for the year, with the same tax engine. Ordinary: the person’s income, with the OAS repayment (the recovery tax, which can also take back that year’s GIS and Allowance) on that year’s own income. Final: the same plus the whole RRIF balance and the taxable part of unsold gains; the OAS repayment is recomputed on that income (and deducted from it); unused net capital losses carried to the end of the death year, plus any deemed loss on unsold units, reduce taxable income, even against other income (the terminal-loss rule). Losses of later years are never used. Both returns go through the same income-tax calculation as the cash flow, including household-tested provincial credits and reductions. Tax at death = (tax + OAS repayment) on the final return − the same on the ordinary one; it can be negative (a refund, for example from a terminal loss), which adds to the estate. In Quebec, the senior assistance credit for the year is worked out again on the final return’s family net income (the spouse’s ordinary income, or their final-return income when both die), and any credit lost is added to tax at death. Losses used at death lower taxable income, not net income, so they don’t change it. A surviving spouse’s own credit isn’t part of the estate. Estate = the person’s balances − tax at death − probate fees.
      • What the Account balances and estate chart shows: the rows ticked in the list beside it. The balance bar stacks the ticked accounts (7 Non-registered, 8 RRSP, 9 RRIF, 10 TFSA) in their colours; the Estate for heirs bar stands beside it and always counts all accounts, whichever are ticked. Either bar alone takes the full width. Each row shows its year-end value this year for the view chosen. Show amounts in draws both bars, and the card, in each year’s dollars or in today’s dollars. The scale fits what is ticked, and a year’s card lists only the ticked items: each account, then their total (“Total investment balance” when all four are ticked, “Total of the accounts shown” otherwise). The choices are kept with the plan, its cases and the cases file.
      • Probate fees (estate administration tax), as of January 2026, on the person’s Non-registered balance at the end of the year: the RRSP, RRIF and TFSA are assumed to name beneficiaries, so they pass outside the will. Where a rate is “per $1,000 or portion”, the excess is rounded up. The dollar thresholds are set in law and not indexed, so later years use them as they are. ON: $15 per $1,000 above $50,000. BC: $6 per $1,000 from $25,000 to $50,000, then $14 per $1,000. AB: $35 up to $10,000, $135 to $25,000, $275 to $125,000, $400 to $250,000, then $525. SK: $7 per $1,000. MB: none (abolished in 2020). QC: none, assuming a notarial will. NB: $25 to $100 up to $20,000, then $5 per $1,000 of the whole value. NS: $85.60 up to $10,000, $215.20 to $25,000, $358.15 to $50,000, $1,002.65 to $100,000, then $16.95 per $1,000 above $100,000. PE: $50 up to $10,000, $100 to $25,000, $200 to $50,000, $400 to $100,000, then $4 per $1,000 above $100,000. NL: $60, plus $0.60 per $100 above $1,000. YT: none up to $25,000, then $140. NT: $30, $110, $215, $325, then $435 above $250,000. NU: the same steps, then $425.
      • Simplifications: court filing fees (for example $200 in BC and Saskatchewan), the capital-gains-deduction adjustment to terminal losses and survivor rollovers are not included.
      Worst, Median and Best
      • Percentiles of the simulated distribution: Worst = 5th (only 1 market in 20 does worse), Median = 50th (the middle outcome: half of simulated values are above it and half below; not a “most likely” value), Best = 95th (only 1 market in 20 does better). Chosen separately for each person and account, in Investment accounts.
      • Withdrawals are those that reach your points in the selected outcome. If an outcome can’t reach a point even with no withdrawals, the point is shown at the highest reachable value and the withdrawal is zero. Switching outcomes never changes the stored points.
      • The Account balances and estate total (all four accounts ticked) adds each account’s balance at its selected percentile. Because the accounts share the same simulated market years, their good and bad years line up, so the sum is close to, but not exactly, the percentile of the combined portfolio.
      • Today’s dollars = nominal amount ÷ (1 + inflation)^(year − 2026).
      Data download
      • Rows: one row per case and year, for the cases picked under Cases (the plan on screen and any saved cases, in Planned Cases’ order). Each case is worked out once with its own settings, each account in its own outcome (Worst, Median or Best) and the Non-registered account with its strategy, so the figures are the ones the app shows for that case and Planned Cases adds up.
      • Always included: Case_Name, Case_Number (empty for the plan on screen), Case_Saved_At, Year, each person’s age, the household settings, and each account’s product (its name, or Custom) and metrics: average annual capital gain, standard deviation, distribution yield, outcome, and the Non-registered portfolio management strategy.
      • Groups: Spending, Income, Investment contributions, Investment balances, Cash flow and tax, and Account balances and estate, each with its own list of details. A figure offered in two groups (an account’s year-end balance, the RRSP deduction, the income and account notes) appears once.
      • Withdrawals: each account has its planned withdrawal (RRSP: planned outflow), what your plan sets for the year, next to the withdrawal paid. They differ only in a year the account runs down to $0 in its outcome. The RRIF also has its required minimum, the part of the withdrawal above the minimum (what you chose to take beyond it), and any minimum the account couldn’t pay. Non-registered, RRSP and TFSA withdrawals have no minimum.
      • OAS clawback: the recovery tax takes back OAS first, then GIS and the Allowance. The download gives the total, its two parts (OAS_Clawback, GIS_and_Allowance_Recovery), and OAS before and after the clawback.
      • Headers: words joined with “_”, starting with whose figure it is: You_, Spouse_ or Household_; settings shared by the plan have none (Province, Year). Units other than dollars end the name (_Percent, _Yes_or_No). In today’s dollars every amount’s header ends with _in_2026_Dollars.
      • Couples and singles: You and Spouse are side by side. A single person’s Spouse columns are empty, and are left out when no picked case has a spouse. Household columns hold the household’s figures, so a column total is never doubled.
      • Amounts: in each year’s dollars, or in today’s dollars with each case’s own inflation (amount ÷ (1 + inflation)^(year − 2026)), rounded to the whole dollar after converting. Notes keep their line names (“Housing: …”), with line breaks shown as “ / ”.
      • File: UTF-8 CSV that opens directly in Excel; the choices made in the panel last until the page is reloaded and aren’t saved with plans or cases files.
      Main limitations
      • This app is designed for desktop and laptop computers. It isn’t designed for phones or other small-screen mobile devices.
      • Whole-year timing; no exact dates, payment months or partial first years.
      • A cases file must follow the cases file template, the structure of the built-in demo file: every field it has, nothing more, each of the right kind (a version field, if any, is ignored; an account’s product name may be empty, Plan’s list of its own points is there only when it has some, and the Taxable interest and Canadian dividends lines only when they’re used, so a file that uses them opens only in v1.1.0 and later), with values the app itself could have made. Files missing a part of the plan (notes, for example) aren’t loaded, and the format is never converted.
      • A plan saved in an earlier year (each case by its own saved date) is carried forward to this year when it loads: each line’s first point becomes what the saved plan had for this year (incomes, spending and contributions as its lines drew them; account balances as it projected them at the end of last year), points, notes and Plan’s marks in past years go, the plan keeps its last year, and amounts in today’s dollars move to this year’s. A CPP or OAS already being paid keeps what the plan paid this year. Its people keep their real years of birth, so they can be older than 71 (up to 100). A plan with fewer than 5 years left runs 5 years, the shortest plan, so its last year moves later; one whose last year has passed isn’t loaded; and a file with no plan still running isn’t loaded at all. A carried Non-registered balance starts with no built-up gain and no capital losses carried from earlier years (like any first balance), so later tax on that account can be a little low. The status line says what was carried, made longer or left out; update the balances from your statements. A file saved in a later year than the computer’s date isn’t loaded. The built-in demo cases instead move with the calendar: every year in them shifts to this one, so their people keep their ages.
      • No CPP/QPP sharing or payroll deductions. (A couple’s pension income splitting is modelled: see Income tax.)
      • The spouse or common-law partner amount isn’t claimed. A couple where one partner has little or no income may pay less tax than the app shows. Quebec’s amount for a person living alone isn’t claimed either, so a single Quebec senior living alone may pay a little less provincial tax.
      • RRSP: annuity purchases and spousal-RRSP attribution are not modelled; money leaving an RRSP before 71 is either a direct transfer to the RRIF or a taxable withdrawal. After the last RRSP contribution, 100% of what leaves moves to the RRIF until your next RRSP point. A plan saved by an earlier version of the app keeps the % it set for those years, and the card of the last contribution year says so.
      • Contributions: RRSP and TFSA contribution room isn’t checked; contributions start in the current year and can’t restart once stopped; an RRSP deduction larger than the year’s income isn’t carried forward; no withdrawal can be planned from an account in a year it receives a contribution.
      • All Non-registered distributions are treated as eligible Canadian dividends; foreign income, interest or return of capital are not modelled separately.
      • Canadian dividends (4) are eligible dividends. Dividends from small private companies (other than eligible) and foreign dividends go in Other taxable income (5): taxed in full, with no gross-up or dividend tax credit. For the first, this overstates the tax a little; for foreign dividends, the foreign tax credit isn’t modelled.
      • Taxable interest (3) and Canadian dividends (4) are for savings held outside the accounts you enter here; the app can’t tell if the same income is entered twice.
      • Non-registered portfolio management strategies are simplified: Hold all time (gains taxed only on units sold, at average cost) or Realize gains every year (gains and losses taxed yearly). Realizing a loss while staying invested assumes a similar but not identical investment is bought.
      • Probate fees are estimated on the Non-registered balance only; a home and other assets aren’t modelled, and accounts without a named beneficiary would add to them. Survivor rollovers are not modelled.
      • Household costs and contributions are compared with net income; a shortfall doesn’t draw more from your accounts or lower the contributions. Costs are household-wide, not split between spouses.
      • The cost averages are national, not provincial, and are estimates for a typical senior couple or single senior, not your own budget; the couple and single split is itself an estimate. Housing blends renters and owners, with and without a mortgage.
      • Tax on Non-registered income is paid from your cash; nothing sells units to cover it, so a year with large reinvested income and little other cash can show net income below $0 until you plan a withdrawal.
      • First-year GIS, the Allowance and the provincial top-ups (other than Quebec’s senior assistance) use the first year’s income in place of the two years before it.
      • Every tax and benefit amount rises each year with your inflation assumption. In law a few don’t: the $2,000 pension income amount, the GIS work exemption ($5,000, then half of the next $10,000), Ontario’s two top brackets and its health premium thresholds, and brackets a province freezes (Manitoba’s, and British Columbia’s for 2027–2030). So far-off years may show a little less tax, or a little more GIS, than the law would give.
      • The federal Canada employment amount isn’t claimed, so a year with employment income may show up to about $210 more federal tax for that person.
      • GIS: the Old Age Security Act’s adjustment for an unused dividend tax credit isn’t modelled.
      • Provincial top-ups use each program’s main single and couple figures with straight-line phase-outs; Manitoba’s and BC’s follow their tables only approximately, and only the homeowner, renter or lodge rates of the Alberta Seniors Benefit are modelled.

      Main sources: Canada Revenue Agency, Service Canada, Retraite Québec, Income Tax Regulations s. 7308, provincial finance ministries, provincial and territorial probate fee legislation, and Statistics Canada (Survey of Household Spending 2023, tables 11-10-0227-01 and 11-10-0224-01; Consumer Price Index, table 18-10-0004-01; 2021 Census, table 98-10-0134-01).
